machine: Apple M4 Pro, macOS Darwin 25.6, 12 logical cores (8P+4E), CPython 3.14.6 (GIL), Go 1.26.5, Rust 1.97.1
exclusivity: exclusive box; load average 1.9-3.4 (idle baseline ~2.4 on this desktop) for every measurement below

does_the_share_still_pay.reading: SOUND HALF: dropping the share unlocks 6-way instead of 5-way-behind-a-serial-donor parallelism, and that is worth a measured 1.79x in Rust (3.375 s -> 1.883 s). UNSOUND HALF: the Build phase read this as 'a packed rewrite makes the share stop paying'. It is not a language finding -- see k1_meso_share_value_per_language, where the model's share is worth 1.7% in Python, 4.1% in Rust and 7.0% in Go. The model's share never paid in any language, so the model cannot price this trade-off. The real kernel's in-cold-build share value is unmeasured anywhere.

corrections_to_the_build_phase.claim: fidelity ratio 0.904 (cost per kernel op), 'treat 21x as 19-23x'
corrections_to_the_build_phase.measured_here: 0.754 median of 3 reps (0.733-0.772). The model's Python is 1.33x CHEAPER per kernel operation than the real kernel, not 1.10x.
corrections_to_the_build_phase.consequence: the fidelity gap is 3x wider than claimed. The direction argument still holds (a wider gap makes the reported multiplier more of a floor), but the band on the headline widens from 19-23x to roughly 20-27x, and the residual uncertainty is larger than the Build phase stated.

corrections_to_the_build_phase.claim: 'in a packed rewrite the share stops paying'
corrections_to_the_build_phase.measured_here: the model's cross-configuration share is worth 1.7% in Python, 4.1% in Rust, 7.0% in Go (L=12, identical per-config checksums both ways).
corrections_to_the_build_phase.consequence: REFUTED as a language finding. The share is weak in the MODEL, in every language including Python. What survives is the structural fact that a serial donor caps parallelism at 5-way, worth a measured 1.79x in Rust -- but whether giving up the real share to get it is a win is not answerable from this model.

corrections_to_the_build_phase.claim: python-six 227.7 CPU-s / 246.2 s wall, rust-six 13.83 s, headline 21.0x one-config
corrections_to_the_build_phase.measured_here: on an exclusive box python-six is 181.6 s wall and rust-six 9.05 s; one-config Rust is 18.2x, six-config 20.1x.
corrections_to_the_build_phase.consequence: the contended figures were roughly self-consistent; the clean numbers are lower in absolute terms and slightly lower in ratio for one config. No conclusion changes.

corrections_to_the_build_phase.claim: Go is consistently 1.3-1.4x slower than Rust on this workload
corrections_to_the_build_phase.measured_here: 1.21x at one config, 1.25x at six -- but the gap WIDENS with problem size (Go is 18.3x of Python at 75k windows and 15.0x at 429k, while Rust is flat at 20.7x -> 19.8x).
corrections_to_the_build_phase.consequence: Go's multiplier is volume-dependent on this workload and the real kernel is 1.6x larger again than the largest model instance, so Go's real-kernel figure should be read as an upper bound. Rust's is not volume-dependent over the range measured.

k1_meso_multiplier_vs_problem_size.note: one config, single-threaded, wall seconds inside the fixpoint; tests whether the language multiplier is an artifact of one model size
k1_meso_multiplier_vs_problem_size.reading: Rust is flat at 19.8-20.7x across a 5.7x change in window count; Go decays 18.3 -> 15.0, so extrapolating Go to the real kernel (1.6x more windows again) would push it lower still

k1_meso_share_value_per_language.question: the Build phase concluded 'in a packed rewrite the share stops paying'. This measures the share's value in ALL THREE languages on the same model, to see whether that is a language finding or a property of the model's share.
k1_meso_share_value_per_language.reading: the model's cross-configuration share is worth 1.7% in Python, 4.1% in Rust and 7.0% in Go -- it never paid much in ANY language, so the model cannot support the claim that a rewrite is what made it stop paying. The real kernel's share value inside a cold six-config build is not measured anywhere (the cost model's 337.9 s cold figure already includes it, and its 194.9 s warm figure is the persisted trace STORE, a different mechanism).

independent_anchor_real_kernel.note: run by this phase, not by any runner, via /usr/bin/time -l uv run python raw/perf2/bench/anchor.py

table.note: each kernel's control loop; the interpreter-dispatch floor

weighted_composite.coverage_caveat: The recipe models only primitive operations. Its Python total covers a fraction of the measured six-config build (see sanity_check.ratio_recipe_over_measured); the remainder is interpreter dispatch, Python-level function calls, attribute lookups and list building -- measured separately as the 'loop skeleton' row of the table, whose Rust and Go ratios are LARGER than most primitive ratios here. The composite is therefore a conservative estimate of the language multiplier, not an optimistic one.

sanity_check.note: the recipe's Python total is compared against the measured 337.87 CPU-s of a real six-config table.build_tables run (raw/perf/cost-model.md). A recipe within a factor of ~2 is credible; further off means the recipe, not the ratio, is what to distrust.

equivalence.what_the_checksum_is: sha256 over one line per shaped run: unit, config, signature_digest (sha256 of CPython's repr of the (before pieces, after pieces) tuple) and delta_digest ('d-' + first 12 hex of sha1 of CPython's repr of the config_diff tuple). The ports reproduce CPython repr() text byte for byte, so this is equality of the persisted digests the repo actually stores, not of some looser summary.

python-optimized-digest.note: identical kernel; signature_digest hashes marshal v2 bytes instead of repr text

fidelity_vs_live_fonts.note: InkComparator's default plain Shaper, so four hb.shape calls per row (two per side, one for signature and one for config_diff). The surface build passes shaper_for, whose memo collapses those to two; see shaping_only for the per-row cost of those two.

harfbuzz_floor.note: uharfbuzz, not rewritable — the cost model's largest irreducible floor

amdahl_with_the_harfbuzz_floor.basis: the surface build's real per-row K3 cost with a memoized shaper: the measured Python arithmetic pass plus the measured cost of the two hb.shape calls per row that no rewrite may remove (an independent shaper is the gate's premise).

repr_free_digest_in_the_ports.note: same kernel, signature digest taken over a packed binary encoding rather than repr text; the Rust and Go packings differ from each other so their checksums are not comparable — timing only

filter_table.note: timed on the decompressed 554 MB table with a plain-text destination, so every language measures the same parse+filter+write. The repo's real gz-in/gz-out call is reported separately, with the zlib inflate cost broken out as a native floor.

full_spec_cross_check_IS_CACHED_NOT_RERU.note: Same harness, all 18 runes, default configuration — the real single-configuration M1 build the cost model measured at 77.51 CPU-s. Run once out of band (60-120 CPU-s per variant, too slow for this runner) and read back here. The counts reproduce the cost model's default-config figures exactly: 682,842 windows, 2,667 rules, 197 reachable cells, 3,563 treaty rows. Timings were taken under sibling-agent contention and are indicative; the equivalence verdict is not.

projection.status: DERIVED — cost-model measured endpoints x ratios measured on this slice; not measured at production scale

scenarios.scenario: run the existing serial code on 3.14t, no threading at all
donor first, then five recipients as threads over the same TraceShare, at the fanout efficiency measured on this slice
drop the share, run the six configurations as six threads with a private spec each, at the speedup measured on the six-configuration slice
scenarios.caveat: 6 x 77.51 s is the DERIVED no-share serial cost, assuming every configuration costs what the measured default configuration costs; the share is worth more at production scale (27%) than on this slice (15%), so this scenario is optimistic on the share side and pessimistic on the config-cost side

scenarios.scenario: CEILING: donor plus one recipient, perfect 5-way fanout, zero threading overhead, recipients assumed equal

projection.why_the_ceiling_is_low: the cross-configuration TraceShare has no content until the donor configuration finishes, so the donor is strictly serial ahead of the other five — Amdahl on a 23% serial fraction caps the whole idea near 2.6x however many cores are free
projection.unmeasured: per-recipient configuration times at production scale (the slowest recipient, not the mean, sets the fanout's floor) and whether six concurrent production fixpoints fit in RAM (per-config peak RSS is a measured 3.85 GB)
